and tell them: "I bear this willingly for your sake, oh Queen. You will restore me to wholeness, or at the very least, you alone are enough for me in place of all else." Cherish me with your loving heart alone, and in this way I shall not feel the losses of my reputation, nor even of my life.

*Sorrow.* I am torn apart everywhere in the public squares.

*Reason.* Take it in good part. The common people will make you known, virtue will make you illustrious, and a clear conscience will make you secure.

### Concerning shame over praise bestowed upon the unworthy.
## DIAL. XXVI.

> Praise with restraint, for when you praise wrongfully,
> Should you later condemn, it will be a mark of fickleness.

*Sorrow.* I am accused of having praised an unworthy man.

<note>A large, ornamental initial L marks the start of the response.</note>

*Reason.* That which is evil often arises from a good root. For good and innocent people, such as they themselves are, imagine others to be the same. Hence they are even more prone to praise than they should be; and although I admit that it is wrong to praise the unworthy, it is nonetheless much worse to slander the innocent.

*Sorrow.* I have praised the unworthy.

*Reason.* If you did so knowingly, you are reprehensible; but if you did so in ignorance, you are excusable. It is less of an evil to be deceived than to deceive. For to be deceived is a stranger's act, but to deceive is the specific crime of the deceiver.

*Sorrow.* The praise of another contributes to my own infamy.

*Reason.* On the contrary, it is either your own fault or your own ignorance. For just as there is no praise in the actions of another, so too there is no infamy in them.

*Sorrow.* I grieve greatly for having praised the unworthy.

*Reason.* See to it, then, that you do not often have cause for this same grief. Beware of rushing rashly into praising or slandering. For there is a craving for both—and to speak properly—a disease and a certain itching of the tongue, which is restless and ignorant of quiet. Its bridle and restraint are numbered among the works of the highest perfection, as Scripture says:

<summary>In this dialogue, Reason consoles Sorrow regarding the dangers of uncritical praise, emphasizing that being deceived by the unworthy is a pardonable error while warning against the restless tongue.</summary>
